content: Acmella oleracea, commonly referred to as the toothache plant or paracress, is a flowering herb belonging to the plant family Asteraceae. Its leaves and flower heads contain an analgesic compound called spilanthol, which is known for its numbing effects and has been traditionally used to alleviate toothache. This plant is native to the tropical regions of Brazil and is cultivated in various parts of the world, both as an ornamental plant and occasionally for medicinal purposes. It is a small, upright plant that grows rapidly and produces golden and red flower inflorescences. While it is frost-sensitive, it can survive as a perennial in warmer climates. The plant has been known by several synonyms, including Spilanthes oleracea L. (1767) and Spilanthes acmella auct. non (L.) Murr.. For further details on its synonyms, one can refer to the Plant Name Database entry on Spilanthes. The English common name toothache plant is synonymous with the Swedish name tandvärksplanta, both of which derive from the plant's analgesic alkylamides. The name paracress is associated with the Brazilian state of Pará. In French, it is called brède mafane or cresson de Pará, while in Portuguese, it is known as agrião do Pará or jambú. In culinary applications, small amounts of shredded fresh leaves are used to impart a unique flavor to salads. When cooked, the leaves lose their strong flavor and can be used as leafy greens. Both fresh and cooked leaves are incorporated into dishes in parts of Brazil, often combined with chilies and garlic to enhance flavor and nutritional value. A related species is used in several Southeast Asian dishes. Additionally, consuming portions or whole flowers has been reported to counteract the intense heat of chilies and peppers. The plant has various traditional uses. A decoction or infusion made from its leaves and flowers is recommended for conditions such as stammering, toothache, stomatitis, and throat complaints. Chewing a whole flower bud produces an intense tingling sensation accompanied by excessive salivation. The primary taste-active compounds in the plant are alkylamides, particularly (2E,6Z,8E)-deca-2,6,8-trienoic acid N-isobutylamide, also known as spilanthol. This compound is responsible for the trigeminal and saliva-inducing effects observed in products like Jambu oleoresin, a concentrated extract derived from paracress. Hexane extracts from freshly harvested flowers of S. acmella have been tested for bioactivity against Aedes aegypti larvae and Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm) neonates. Mosquitocidal assays using spilanthol demonstrated significant activity, with a concentration of 25 mg/mL. A mixture of spilanthol isomers caused a 66% weight reduction in H. zea neonate larvae at a concentration of 250 mg/mL after six days. Additionally, Spilanthes acmella has shown strong diuretic effects in rats. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of spilanthol against various yeasts (Candida albicans, C. krusei, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis) and bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) is greater than 1000 μg/mL, indicating limited antimicrobial activity. Beyond spilanthol, the plant contains other bioactive compounds such as stigmasterol, stigmasteryl-3-O-β-D-glucopyranoside, a mixture of triterpenes, and long-chain fatty esters. The isolation and total synthesis of these active ingredients have been documented.
